argument: The episode reads Hamlet the way a philosopher might, setting the traditional take, where a good person in a bad situation stages the collision between medieval, God-rooted moral guidance and Renaissance Humanism, against Simon Critchley and Jamieson Webster's reading in Stay Illusion! The Hamlet Doctrine. Building on Nietzsche's line that knowledge kills action and action requires the veil of illusion, they see Hamlet as an Anti-Oedipus: a man whose insight into the game of morally rationalizing our actions leaves him paralyzed, stuck in an unsustainable internal state that curdles into shame, self-loathing, and lashing out, inside a play structured by surveillance that his own self-analysis mirrors. Against Hamlet stands Ophelia, the play's true tragic hero, a person genuinely capable of love whose madness and death become a heroic truth exposing what the court reduced her to, in a play that is ultimately about nothing in the sense of nihilism, and about how the knowledge we most need can be exactly the knowledge that ruins us.
keyIdeas: The traditional reading sees Hamlet's indecision as Shakespeare staging the collision between medieval moral guidance rooted in God and Renaissance Humanism, where answers are no longer readily available and people must think their way to morality alone.

Following Nietzsche's claim that knowledge kills action and action requires the veil of illusion, Critchley and Webster read Hamlet as an Anti-Oedipus: where Oedipus acts totally in ignorance, Hamlet's knowledge and insight prevent him from ever acting at all.

Rather than a good person in a bad situation, Hamlet is a man stuck in an unsustainable internal state, unable to accept and move on and unable to act, whose unmetabolized psychological energy turns into shame, self-loathing, and lashing out at everyone around him.

Where traditional readings see the play's spying as reflecting Elizabethan England's emerging surveillance state, Critchley and Webster intensify this into surveillance as a structural condition of the play, with Hamlet's constant self-surveillance mirroring the omnipresent espionage around him.

Ophelia, compared to Antigone as a woman treated as an object by a king and the men around her, is the play's true tragic hero: genuinely capable of love where Hamlet, fleeing every need into his head, embodies Dostoevsky's hell as the inability to love, her death becomes a love-act exposing what the court reduced her to, in a play about nothing in the sense of nihilism.

terms.def: Critchley and Webster's name for the idea that knowledge and insight have, in practice, the ability to kill people's capacity to take action in the world.
Their description of Hamlet as the inverse of Oedipus: where Oedipus acts totally in ignorance and learns the truth later, Hamlet's knowledge prevents him from ever acting in the first place.
The post-medieval outlook Shakespeare wrote in the wake of, where moral answers rooted in God are no longer easily available and people must battle toward them in their own minds.
Critchley and Webster's term for the generic, traditional readings of the play, the kind that gets you an A on a school test without shaking anything up.
Their term for Ophelia's madness and death: her only remaining language of exchange, a heroic truth exposing what the court's schemes had worked to reduce her to.
The Lacanian idea that love is always built on incompleteness and need, requiring a vulnerability that Hamlet never allows into his life.

anchors: this was Shakespeare staging the tension that goes ON…when EARLIER, MEDIEVAL forms of moral guidance rooted in something like a god…collides with LATER, Renaissance Humanism…where these answers AREN’T as easily available to people, and so CREATE people who are stuck in a battle up in their own minds.
Hamlet is someone who can’t ACT…because he LACKS the moral illusions to justify what he wants to do.

Oedipus, then, is someone that ACTS totally in ignorance, despite not knowing much of anything…and to Webster and Critchley HAMLET…is the ANTI-Oedipus, he’s a man whose KNOWLEDGE of his father’s death and his insights about the moral game most of us are playing…PREVENT him from EVER taking action in the first place.
ALL this excess psychological energy that can’t be metabolized…gets transformed through his behavior in the play into the shame we see, self-loathing, melancholy about his situation.
Hamlet’s world is a globe defined by the omnipresence of espionage, of which his self-surveillance is but a mirror.
Her madness and her death, BECOME a kind of heroic TRUTH in the play…because they expose what the world has worked so hard to reduce her to…nothing.
She also, was treated COMPLETELY as an object by a King…not to mention by all the OTHER men around her.

Hamlet is reduced to nothing because he is trapped in a state of paralysis where he can’t accept and can’t move forward. Ophelia is reduced to nothing by the men and schemes that USE her that are all around her.
he DOES all this…just so he doesn’t ever have to show anyone else any sort of NEED that he may be having.
The character of Hamlet shows us…that sometimes the knowledge we MOST NEED…is the VERY knowledge that RUINS us the MOST… at an existential level, and at the level of identity.
